paper_title: On-Policy Morphing into Hybrid Attention Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Hybrid attention models combine full and linear attention to achieve a better quality--efficiency trade-off. Converting pretrained Transformers into such models requires identifying which layers should retain full attention under a prescribed budget. We identify two off-policy mismatches in FlashMorph's layer selection: (i) continuous branch interpolation and teacher-forced hidden states differ from discrete hybrid computation; and (ii) frozen model weights fail to account for parameter adaptation during subsequent recovery. We introduce FlashMorph2, an on-policy layer-selection method that (I) evaluates sampled discrete hybrid architectures end to end using their own hidden states, and (II) jointly optimizes layer-selection scores and model weights under the recovery objective to reflect post-adaptation performance. Experiments across Qwen3 model scales and linear-attention variants show that FlashMorph2 consistently outperforms existing layer-selection methods, improving average scores over FlashMorph by $+2.42$ points on RULER, $+1.08$ on LongBench, and $+0.76$ on recall-intensive tasks, while completing layer selection in only $0.72$--$3.57$ GPU hours across 0.6B--8B models, demonstrating high efficiency and scalability.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Hybrid attention models combine full and linear attention to achieve better qualityefficiency trade-off. Converting pretrained Transformers into such models requires identifying which layers should retain full attention under prescribed budget. We identify two off-policy mismatches in FlashMorphs layer selection: (i) continuous branch interpolation and teacher-forced hidden states differ from discrete hybrid computation; and (ii) frozen model weights fail to account for parameter adaptation during subsequent recovery. We introduce FlashMorph2, an on-policy layerselection method that (I) evaluates sampled discrete hybrid architectures end to end using their own hidden states, and (II) jointly optimizes layerselection scores and model weights under the recovery objective to reflect post-adaptation performance. Experiments across Qwen3 model scales and linear-attention variants show that FlashMorph2 consistently outperforms existing layerselection methods, improving average scores over FlashMorph by +2.42 points on RULER, +1.08 on LongBench, and +0.76 on recall-intensive tasks, while completing layer selection in only 0.723.57 GPU hours across 0.6B8B models, demonstrating high efficiency and scalability. 1. Introduction Hybrid attention models retain full attention in only few layers and use linear attention elsewhere, preserving longcontext modeling capabilities and precise retrieval (Arora et al., 2024a; Jelassi et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026a), while substantially reducing computation and KV-cache memory usage (Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2025b;a). Owing to this favorable trade-off between performance and efficiency, hybrid attention has been adopted in growing number of production-scale large language models (LLMs) (Li *Work done at ByteDance Seed 1Fudan University 2ByteDance Seed 3Nanyang Technological University. Correspondence to: Yu Cheng <yu.cheng@ntu.edu.sg>. Preprint. Figure 1. Comparison between FlashMorph and FlashMorph2. FlashMorph uses off-policy teacher-forced continuous gates with frozen model weights, whereas FlashMorph2 samples on-policy discrete hybrid architectures and jointly optimizes layer-selection scores and model weights. et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025; Cao et al., 2026; Team, 2026; Team et al., 2026). To avoid the prohibitive cost of pretraining from scratch, existing approaches reuse the weights of pretrained LLMs and replace subset of full attention layers with linear attention, achieving Transformers-to-hybrid conversion. Model quality is then recovered through distillation and continued training (Kasai et al., 2021; Bick et al., 2024; Lan et al., 2025; Goldstein et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024; Bick et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). central challenge in this conversion process is determining which full attention layers to retain under given budget. As the only layers in the resulting hybrid model that can directly access the entire context, their placement largely determines how much of the original models capability can be recovered (Li et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026; Lan et al., 2026). Exhaustively evaluating all possible layer combinations is prohibitively expensive, motivating existing work to explore variety of layer-selection strategies. Beyond fixed uniform interleaving patterns, PostNAS (Gu et al., 2026) performs supernet-based architecture search, KL-LS (Li et al., 2026a) ranks layers by the KL reduction from per-layer restoration and distillation, and HALO (Chen et al., 2026) uses replacement-based sensitivity scoring. More recently, FlashMorph (Lan et al., 2026) jointly optimizes layer-wise gates On-Policy Morphing into Hybrid Attention Models to learn global hybrid configuration. Each layer interpolates between aligned fulland linear-attention branches through continuous gate, which is then discretized under given full-attention budget. FlashMorph preserves strong long-context recall and general benchmark performance while substantially reducing layer-selection cost. Limitations. FlashMorphs layer-selection process still suffers from two forms of off-policy mismatch. (L1) Offpolicy computation: The forward computation used during layer selection differs from that of the candidate discrete model. Continuous mixing allows the fulland linearattention branches to complement each other, while each layer operates on teacher-forced hidden states. At deployment, only one branch is retained per layer and hidden states are generated by the hybrid model itself. Consequently, complementarities observed under continuous mixing may not transfer to the final discrete architecture, and the resulting layer-importance estimates may fail to capture error accumulation and cross-layer compensation. (L2) Off-policy weights: The weights used for layer selection are inherited from the original model and remain frozen during gate optimization, without adapting to the hybrid architecture induced by the selection policy. Layer selection therefore cannot account for the cross-layer co-adaptation of model weights during subsequent recovery, which may alter the layer-importance ranking observed before recovery. Our Method. We introduce FlashMorph2, which improves upon FlashMorph by bringing the on-policy principle into its layer-selection process. To address (L1), FlashMorph2 samples discrete hybrid attention architecture that satisfies the prescribed full-attention budget and performs an end-to-end forward pass through the sampled architecture, allowing each layer to operate on hidden states produced by the model itself. To address (L2), FlashMorph2 jointly trains model weights across these sampled hybrid attention architectures using the same optimization objective as in subsequent recovery training, allowing layer selection to account for performance after weight adaptation. Results. Across Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B backbones and three linear-attention variants, FlashMorph2 consistently outperforms all layer-selection baselines, improving average scores over FlashMorph by +2.42 points on RULER, +1.08 on LongBench, and +0.76 on recallintensive tasks while preserving language modeling and commonsense reasoning capabilities. Moreover, FlashMorph2 completes layer selection in only 0.723.57 GPU hours across 0.6B8B models, running 8.420.8 faster than HALO and 560854 faster than KL-LS. Contributions. Our key contributions are as follows: We identify two forms of off-policy mismatch in FlashMorphs layer selection: (I) continuous interpolation and teacher-forced hidden states differ from deployed discrete hybrid computation, and (II) scores computed with frozen weights fail to reflect the optimal layer ranking after recovery training. We introduce FlashMorph2, an on-policy layer selection method for Transformer-to-hybrid conversion that performs end-to-end forward passes through sampled hybrid architectures under full-attention budget, allowing selection to account for self-generated hidden states and weights adapted under the recovery objective. We evaluate FlashMorph2 across multiple Qwen3 model scales and linear-attention variants, demonstrating consistent improvements on long-context and recallintensive benchmarks while maintaining high layerselection efficiency and scalability. 2. Related Work Layer Selection for Transformer-to-hybrid Conversion. Transformer-to-hybrid conversion requires selecting which full-attention layers to retain under prescribed budget. simple solution is fixed uniform interleaving (Lan et al., 2025; Goldstein et al., 2025), but it ignores layer-wise heterogeneity in pretrained models. PostNAS (Gu et al., 2026) trains once-for-all supernet and uses task-guided beam search to determine full-attention layer placement, incurring substantial training and search costs; KL-LS (Li et al., 2026a) ranks layers by post-distillation KL loss after singlelayer restoration; and HALO (Chen et al., 2026) ranks fullattention layers by the downstream performance changes induced by their individual replacement with linear-attention layers. These layerwise scoring methods incur substantial selection overhead from repeated single-layer evaluations and fail to account for interactions among layers in the resulting hybrid architecture. FlashMorph (Lan et al., 2026) jointly optimizes layerwise gate values, yielding more effective hybrid configurations at substantially lower selection cost. However, these methods remain off-policy due to mismatches in forward computation or model weights between the selection-time and recovered hybrid models. FlashMorph2 improves upon FlashMorph with on-policy layer selection that performs end-to-end forward passes through sampled discrete hybrid architectures while accounting for the effects of weight adaptation during recovery. On-Policy Learning. Teacher forcing relies on groundtruth prefixes and is therefore off-policy with respect to the models own generation policy; the resulting train-inference distribution mismatch can lead to exposure bias and error accumulation (Bengio et al., 2015). To mitigate this distribution shift, on-policy learning emphasizes obtaining supervision on states induced by the learners own policy (Ross et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2020). Following this principle, on-policy distillation (OPD) trains students under teacher supervision on sequences generated by the students them2 On-Policy Morphing into Hybrid Attention Models selves (Lu & Lab, 2025; Li et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2026). FlashMorph2 extends this idea to layer selection by sampling discrete hybrid architectures and estimating layer importance using self-generated hidden states and weights adapted under the recovery objective. 3. FlashMorph Pipeline FlashMorph (Lan et al., 2026) builds on the staged distillation pipeline of RADLADS (Goldstein et al., 2025) and HALO (Chen et al., 2026) for Transformer-to-hybrid conversion. Rethinking FlashMorph Layer selection objective. FlashMorph formulates layer selection as subset selection problem that maximizes hybrid model performance under fixed full-attention budget (Lan et al., 2026). Since the quality of selected layers also depends on subsequent recovery training, we evaluate selected architectures based on their post-recovery performance: = arg max ICK Score (cid:0)M(I; θ)(cid:1), (9) where θ denotes the model parameters of the selected hybrid architecture obtained after initialization from θ0 and subsequent recovery training, and Score() measures postrecovery task performance. Individually recovering and evaluating all (cid:0) (cid:1) hybrid architectures is prohibitively expensive. FlashMorph therefore uses Eq. 6 as proxy for layer selection before recovery. However, this proxy has two off-policy limitations that prevent it from fully reflecting the post-recovery performance of the resulting hybrid model: L1: Off-policy computation. During FlashMorphs layer selection, continuous gates mix fulland linear-attention outputs computed from teacher hidden states (Eqs.5 and 6). The deployed model instead uses discrete hybrid architecture under the prescribed full-attention budget, retaining one branch per layer and propagating its own hidden states (Eq.3). Thus, rankings learned under continuous mixing can misrepresent layer importance in the discrete hybrid architecture, while teacher-forced layerwise evaluation fails to capture how hidden-state deviations induced by attention replacement propagate through subsequent hybrid layers. L2: Off-policy weights. Eq. 6 performs layer selection by optimizing continuous gates while keeping model weights frozen at their pre-recovery values θ0, whereas Eq.9 evaluates discrete hybrid architectures using the recovered parameters θ. Since the frozen weights have not been adapted to the candidate hybrid architectures, subsequent recovery may alter the layer-importance ranking, potentially rendering the initial selection suboptimal. These two forms of off-policy limitation highlight the need for layer selection to jointly account for end-to-end forward computation and weight adaptation on discrete hybrid architectures satisfying the prescribed full-attention budget. Building on this insight, Sec. 4 introduces our proposed FlashMorph2s on-policy layer-selection method. 4. Methodology Drawing on on-policy learning, FlashMorph2 refines FlashMorphs optimization-based layer selection. Specifically, as illustrated in Fig. 2, FlashMorph2 samples discrete hybrid configurations satisfying the prescribed full-attention budget, performs end-to-end forward computation with selfpropagated hidden states rather than teacher-forced hidden states, and jointly optimizes the layer-selection parameters and model weights using the same training objective as in the subsequent recovery stage to guide the layer selection. 4.1. Gumbel(0, 1). gl (10) We employ Gumbel-Top-K sampling trick without replacement (Kool et al., 2019), selecting exactly distinct fullattention layers per sample, with higher layer-selection scores corresponding to higher selection probabilities. We denote the induced distribution over hybrid architectures in CK by qϕ, with the corresponding binary mask defined as ml = 1[l I]. All layer-selection scores are initialized to the same constant, ensuring no prior preference for any layer during initial sampling. Given sampled mask, the model performs an on-policy forward pass through the corresponding discrete hybrid architecture (Eq. 3). Each layer operates on hidden states propagated through the sampled architecture and uses the output of its selected attention branch, allowing earlier branch choices to affect subsequent layer inputs and ultimately the final predictions. Layer-selection evaluation thus captures error accumulation and cross-layer compensation induced by attention replacement through forward computation consistent with that of the deployed hybrid architecture. 4 On-Policy Morphing into Hybrid Attention Models Figure 2. Overview of FlashMorph2. Following layerwise alignment, FlashMorph2 constructs hybrid attention model through on-policy layer selection, jointly optimizing layer scores and model weights over sampled discrete hybrid architectures. The resulting hybrid attention model is further trained using logits distillation and long-context finetuning to recover model quality. 4.2. On-Policy Weight Adaptation To account for weight adaptation during subsequent recovery, we initialize the student model with the layerwise aligned parameters θ0 and jointly optimize the layerselection parameters ϕ and model weights θ over sampled hybrid architectures: min ϕ, θ (ϕ, θ) = EIqϕ (cid:104) LKD(θ; I) (cid:105) , (11) where LKD(θ; I) denotes the logits distillation objective used in subsequent recovery training stage (Eq. 7), computed on the currently sampled hybrid architecture I. All sampled hybrid architectures are constructed by selecting attention branches from shared morphable model, directly reusing the parameters of the selected branches. During layer-selection optimization, we compute the distillation loss on sampled architectures and obtain gradients for both the layer-selection parameters ϕ and model weights θ through single backward pass. The layer-selection parameters are updated via gradient straight-through estimator (STE) (Bengio et al., 2013; Jang et al., 2016) (Sec. 4.3) to adjust the architecture-sampling distribution. For each sampled architecture, unselected attention branches receive no gradients. As the model weights continuously adapt to the sampled hybrid architectures, the layer-selection parameters are updated based on the corresponding optimization signals. This on-policy layer-selection method incorporates weight adaptation into architecture evaluation, mitigating the discrepancy between frozen-weight layer evaluation and post-recovery performance. After optimization, we remove the sampling noise and select the final full-attention layers as = TopK(ϕ, K). To isolate the effect of layer selection, we retain only the selected architecture, reinitialize M(I ; θ0) with the original parameters θ0, and apply the same Stage 3-4 recovery training pipeline. The model weights θ updated during Stage 2 serve only to guide layer selection and are not used to initialize subsequent recovery training. 4.3. We further evaluate performance on 6 recall-intensive tasks using the prefix-linear-attention evaluation suite (Arora et al., 2024b). We also evaluate language modeling perplexity and zero-shot commonsense reasoning using lmevaluation-harness (Gao et al., 2024). All evaluations are conducted using vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) for accelerated inference. Detailed evaluation settings are also provided in the Appendix B. Baselines. We compare FlashMorph2 against five layer selection baselines, including: uniform interleaving (Uniform), PostNAS (Gu et al., 2026), KL-LS (Li et al., 2026a), HALO (Chen et al., 2026), and FlashMorph (Lan et al., 2026). To isolate the effect of layer selection, all methods use the same full-attention budget, layerwise-aligned initialization, and subsequent recovery training settings. 5.2. Main Results Long-context capabilities. Table 1 reports long-context performance under the same full-attention budget. FlashMorph2 achieves the highest average scores on both RULER and LongBench across all six combinations of backbone size and linear-attention variant. Averaged across these configurations, it raises the RULER score from 63.26 to 65.68 (+2.42 points) and the LongBench score from 29.86 to 30.94 (+1.08 points) compared with FlashMorph. These results demonstrate that FlashMorph2 identifies hybrid architectures with consistently superior long-context performance following an identical recovery training settings. Recall-intensive tasks. Table 2 reports performance on six recall-intensive tasks. FlashMorph2 achieves the highest average score across tasks in all six combinations of backbone size and linear-attention variant. Averaged across these configurations, it improves the score from 48.94 to 49.70 (+0.76 points) compared with FlashMorph. These results indicate that the benefits of FlashMorph2 extend to real-world in-context retrieval tasks. Language modeling and commonsense reasoning. Table 9 in the Appendix reports language modeling perplexity and zero-shot commonsense reasoning accuracy. FlashMorph2 remains competitive with the layer-selection baselines on these evaluations, suggesting that general language capabilities are preserved alongside the improvements in long-context and recall-intensive tasks. 5.3. Analysis Layer-selection efficiency. Fig. 3 reports the computational cost of layer selection across different model scales. Compared with FlashMorph, FlashMorph2 requires 1.72.6 the FLOPs and 1.92.4 the GPU hours, reflecting the additional computation required for end-to-end evaluation of discrete hybrid architectures and concurrent model adaptation. This overhead is confined to one-time selection 7 On-Policy Morphing into Hybrid Attention Models Figure 3. Layer-selection Efficiency across Model Scales. Comparison of (a) FLOPs and (b) GPU hours required for layer selection across Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 8B parameters. Figure 4. RULER Performance across Hybrid Ratios. Average RULER scores on the Qwen3-1.7B backbone across varying hybrid ratios for (a) GLA and (b) GDN variants. stage, which accounts for approximately only < 1% of the overall conversion token budget, and does not affect deployment efficiency under the same full-attention budget. Across models ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters, FlashMorph2 completes layer selection in only 0.723.57 GPU hours. It is also substantially more efficient than layerwise-scoring approaches. Relative to FlashMorph2, HALO requires 1.3 2.2 as many FLOPs and 8.420.8 as many GPU hours, while KL-LS requires 575897 and 560854 as many, respectively. Overall, despite its modest overhead over FlashMorph, FlashMorph2 remains highly efficient and scalable while being substantially more efficient than alternative layer-selection methods. Hybrid ratios. Fig. 4 reports RULER performance on Qwen3-1.7B across different hybrid ratios for GLA and GDN. While full linearization (1:0) reduces the RULER score from 87.66 to 9.57 on GLA and 21.89 on GDN, retaining small subset of full-attention layers substantially restores retrieval performance. Across all evaluated hybrid ratios (6:1, 3:1, and 1:1), FlashMorph2 consistently outperforms all baselines on both linear-attention variants. The advantage of optimization-based layer selection is particularly pronounced under the tightest full-attention budget (6:1), where FlashMorph2 achieves 60.12 on GLA and 64.45 on GDN, outperforming Uniform by +10.65 and +7.86 points while several competing methods fall below simple uniform interleaving. As the full-attention ratio increases to 3:1 and 1:1, performance across methods gradually converges toward the full-attention backbone, yet FlashMorph2 continues to improve upon FlashMorph in all settings, reaching 76.93 on GLA (+1.42) and 80.69 on GDN (+0.92) at 1:1. Overall, these results confirm that FlashMorph2 remains effective and robust across varying hybrid ratios. Ablation study. Table 3 evaluates the effects of on-policy computation and on-policy weight adaptation on Qwen31.7B with GDN. Removing on-policy computation significantly reduces scores by 29.55 points on RULER and 5.71 points on LongBench. Inspecting the selected architectures reveals that this variant allocates all seven full-attention layTable 3. Ablation Study of FlashMorph2. Average RULER and LongBench scores on the Qwen3-1.7B backbone with GDN. Method FlashMorph2 w/o On-Policy Computation w/o On-Policy Weight w/o Both (FlashMorph) RULER LongBench 74.46 44.91 69.58 73. 33.81 28.10 32.43 32.62 ers to the deepest layers {20, 21, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27}, leaving the first 20 layers entirely linear. This concentration reflects the mismatch between teacher-forced local scoring and end-to-end discrete hybrid computation, where early hidden-state deviations accumulate across layers. Removing on-policy weight adaptation instead lowers RULER by 4.88 points and LongBench by 1.38 points, replacing layers {6, 17, 19, 20} selected by FlashMorph2 with {0, 1, 2, 26}, which indicates that weight adaptation substantially alters the preferred budget allocation. Removing both components reverts to FlashMorph, which still trails FlashMorph2 by 1.39 points on RULER and 1.19 points on LongBench. Overall, these results confirm that discrete hybrid computation and weight adaptation are complementary and must be jointly considered during layer selection. 6. Conclusion In this work, we present FlashMorph2, an on-policy layerselection method for converting pretrained Transformers into hybrid attention models under prescribed fullattention budget. To overcome the off-policy computation and weight mismatches in prior optimization-based selection, FlashMorph2 samples discrete budget-constrained hybrid architectures, performs end-to-end forward passes with self-propagated hidden states, and jointly optimizes layerselection scores and model weights under the recovery training objective. Experiments across multiple Qwen3 model scales, linear-attention variants, and hybrid ratios show that FlashMorph2 consistently improves long-context and recallintensive performance over existing baselines while maintaining high selection efficiency and scalability. On-Policy Morphing into Hybrid Attention Models A. Experimental Details A.1. Model Configurations Table 4 summarizes the model architectural specifications of the Qwen3 backbones (Yang et al., 2025a) and their corresponding hybrid attention models under the default 3:1 linear-to-full attention hybrid ratio. To convert grouped-query attention (GQA) in the pretrained full-attention layers into multi-head linear attention (MHA), we expand the pretrained key and value projection weights by repeating each KV head across its corresponding query group during initialization, while directly reusing the pretrained query and output projection weights. Each linear-attention branch is further equipped with RMSNorm on queries, keys, and branch outputs, an element-wise sigmoid output gate initialized to zero, and rotary position embeddings (RoPE) (Su et al., 2024). All newly introduced parameters in the linear-attention branches (e.g., decay/forget gates and output gates) are trained from scratch starting in Stage 1. Training Configurations Table 5 summarizes the training hyperparameters across all four stages of the Transformer-to-hybrid conversion pipeline: layerwise alignment (Stage 1), on-policy layer selection (Stage 2), logits distillation (Stage 3), and long-context finetuning (Stage 4). All stages are trained on randomly sampled subsets of DCLM (Li et al., 2024) using the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2014) without weight decay. In Stage 1, only the linear-attention branches are updated while all pretrained backbone weights remain frozen. In Stage 2, we initialize all layer-selection scores ϕ to 0.5 and jointly optimize ϕ and the model weights θ under WarmupStableDecay (WSD) (Hu et al., 2024) learning rate schedule. After Stage 2, we retain the top-K full-attention layers, reinitialize the selected hybrid attention model with the Stage 1 weights θ0, and train all model parameters end to end during Stage 3 and Stage 4.
